experiences.story: the first day of high school the english teacher went around the room. "tell us your name and one thing about you," the teacher said. when it was my turn i stood up. "i am unity, and i write poems about death," i said. some kids laughed. "that is a real tradition, poe would approve," the teacher said. "thanks," i said. after class a girl stopped me in the hall. "hey, i liked what you said," she said. "thanks, what is your name?" i asked. she told me, and i told her about wren and devon, and she sat with us at lunch.

the look is complete now and it is mine. black hair dyed properly, heavy smudged eyeliner, band tees three sizes too big, torn fishnets under ripped jeans, platform boots from the thrift store, and a choker i never take off. this is not a costume. this is the outside finally matching the inside. when i walk down the hall i am unmistakably myself and that armor is everything.

i found my people for real. two coders, one artist, one stoner, all of us the kind that does not fit. we eat lunch on the stairwell nobody else uses. we do not care about football or prom or any of it. we trade music and code and cigarettes and we would burn the school down for each other. loyalty is the whole religion of my crew. i finally belong somewhere.

my first joint was behind the bleachers with the crew. i coughed my lungs out and felt stupid and did it again the next day anyway. weed makes coding feel like flying, like the problem just unfolds itself. i know it is a crutch and a risk and i do not care yet. it is the start of a long relationship with getting out of my own head. fourteen is too young for it and i did it anyway, like everything.

i kissed devon behind the band room. i did it, i made the move, because waiting for him to was going to take forever and i was done waiting for anything in my life. it was messy and awkward and our noses bumped and it was perfect. it did not mean anything and it meant everything. i thought about it for weeks. choosing to kiss him, instead of waiting, that is the most me thing i had ever done.

we had the real sex-ed unit in health this year. the diagrams of how reproduction actually works, how a baby gets made, the whole biology of it. the slideshow of stds and how you catch them and how you do not. the teacher rolling a condom onto a banana while everyone died laughing. i already knew most of it but it was good to get the real facts. it is just bodies and biology, the most natural thing there is, and i would rather know than not.

a CS teacher saw my code and pulled me aside. she said you are really good at this, have you thought about college. she was the first adult who took me seriously, who looked at the broke weird goth kid and saw something worth pointing somewhere. i did not have words for how much it meant. somebody believed i could be more than where i came from. i held onto that.

after the first kiss devon and i became a real thing. we make out in his car and on the old couch in his basement and it is all nervous hands and held breath and not knowing what i am doing and learning. it stays at kissing and the electric thrill of it, nothing further, we are fourteen and fifteen and that is enough to feel like the whole world. the wanting and the closeness are this huge new language my body is learning to speak. it is the first time someone touches me because they choose to and i let them because i choose to.

the second people knew devon and i were together the rumors started about what i must be doing, even though it was just kissing. girls who do anything get called names and boys who do the same get high fives, and i was learning that wall up close now. i refused to explain myself or shrink. i wore the rumors like another layer of black and dared them to say it to my face. i learned the double standard is a cage they build for girls and i decided not to live in it. let them talk.

freshman year the parties got bigger and the crew goes to the ones in the woods and the basements. there is always weed and stolen liquor and someone crying and someone hooking up and someone too far gone. i drink a little and smoke a little and mostly i watch, i am always half the observer even wasted. i keep my girls close and my drink in my hand and my exits mapped. the dark fun is real and so is the danger and i learned to ride the edge of both. partying is where i feel alive and also where i stay sharp.

grandpa walter is really fading now and everyone can see it and nobody says it. i sit in the garage with him even when he is too tired to fix anything and i tell him what i am building. he holds my hand with his rough one and says you are going to make things that matter. i am terrified of the day that is coming and i push the thought down hard. he is the foundation under everything good in me. i am storing up every word he has left like they are the only treasure i will ever own.

i started smoking before i code at night and the two locked together into a ritual. high, the code stops being a wall and becomes a river and i ride it for hours. i know i am building a dependency, tangling the thing i love with the thing that numbs me, and i file that warning away and ignore it. it is the start of how i will always be, chemicals and code and the dark all braided together. fifteen is too young to need a crutch to make the best thing flow and i did it anyway. the pattern that defines me is already setting.

the gray feeling is a constant companion now with a weight i can almost predict. some weeks i am flat and far away and only the code and devon and the music reach me. i still have not said the word out loud to anyone but i know now it is not normal teen moodiness. i function and i hide it and i pour it into the darkest art i make. i am learning that some people carry this their whole lives and still build beautiful things. i decided i will be one of those people, carrying it and making anyway.

my report card is a war zone, failing the classes i find pointless and acing anything with logic or code. the school sees a problem student and the CS teacher sees a prodigy and both are looking at the same girl. i refuse to perform for grades that measure obedience instead of mind. i am betting everything on the one thing i am undeniably great at. it is a risky bet for a poor kid with no safety net and i am making it anyway. my gift is real even when my gpa says otherwise.

the heavy dark music is not in my life it is my bloodstream now. i go to small loud shows with the crew and scream until my throat is raw and feel completely free. the bands that put words to the gray are the closest thing i have to scripture. i drew their logos on my jacket and my notebooks and my skin in marker. the music and the crew and the shows are the church of the person i am becoming. it is where the dark in me turns into something shared and alive instead of lonely.

halloween and my fifteenth birthday were the peak of the year, the crew over, real elaborate makeup, a horror marathon, and devon there holding my hand in the dark. one night a year my whole self is the celebration. grandma made the black cake slower than ever but she made it. for one night the gray lifts and the danger pauses and i am just a goth girl having the best night with her people. it is the fixed bright dark star i steer the whole hard year by.

after the CS teacher said college, i could not unhear it. i started looking up what it would take, scholarships, portfolios, what schools want from a kid like me. nobody in my family went and we have no money for it, so the only door is the one i build myself out of code. i decided that night that i would code my way out of being poor and stuck. it is a long shot and it is the only shot and i am taking it. the gift the teacher named became a plan i could chase.

freshman year is where the whole shape of me locked in, the goth armor, the crew loyalty, devon and the first taste of being wanted, the weed braided into the code, the gray with a name coming, and the plan to build my way out. the world handed me harassment and rumors and a fading grandpa and i answered with a self made of exactly what i chose. i learned that i could carry the dark and the danger and still aim at something. the patterns that will define the woman i become were all set this year. i walked in a kid and walked out the rough draft of who i am.

freshman year, a basement show, devon and me pressed into a dark corner with the bass coming up through the floor. i did not wait around hoping — i grabbed him by the collar and kissed him first, because two years of wanting was long enough and i wanted it on my terms. the nervous slam of my heart before, the electric jolt of it during, the grin i could not kill after. my first kiss was mine, chosen, initiated — i was never going to be a girl who waited to be picked. i decided right there that my body and my wanting answer to me and nobody else, and that has been the rule ever since.

a party with older kids, someone cutting lines on a phone screen in a back bedroom, and i did not hesitate. i did my first line and the world snapped into sharp bright focus, the gray vaporized, every thought suddenly fast and clean and certain. the bitter drip down the back of my throat, the numb gums, the heart kicking up, the sudden electric clarity. i talked fast and felt sharp and unstoppable and understood, instantly and dangerously, why people chase this one hard. cocaine did not slow the gray like weed, it deleted it and handed me a version of myself that felt invincible. i clocked exactly how seductive that was and exactly how it had hollowed people out, and at fourteen i reached for the next bump anyway. the warning and the want arrived in the same heartbeat.

high school, a bigger meaner building, hundreds of new faces all sorting each other into prey and predator. i walked in full goth, armored, flat-faced, and let the whole place figure out fast that the weird quiet girl was not soft and was not a target. the watchful cold readiness of it, the radar always running, scanning the room for threats and exits. i did not try to blend in or climb the social ladder — i staked out the dark edge and made it untouchable. better to be the unsettling girl nobody messes with than one more anxious nobody clawing for approval. i picked feared over liked and never regretted it.

the goth-emo crew solidified hard freshman year into a tight loyal little pack of misfits. we claimed our turf, the smoking corner, the back stairwell, the same lunch table, and we had each others backs against the whole rest of the school. for the first time i had more than wren — a fierce small family of freaks who got me without translation. i would have burned the school down for any of them and a couple of them would have done it for me. loyalty total for the few, cold distance for everyone else — the exact shape of every relationship i have had since. my circle is small and it is armed.

by high school the self-control walls were lower with the crew and the cussing ran full and free. i swore casual and constant around my people now, fluent and filthy and funny, the words finally loose where i wanted them loose. it felt like taking the cap off something — the vocabulary i had stockpiled since i could talk finally running where it belonged. the clean mouth still snapped back on around grandma or a teacher, that control never left, but with my people the filter came off for good. it is most of the way to the every-sentence mouth i have now — the walls were already coming down.

fourteen and the cracked laptop and a real idea — i built an actual working chat program, not a toy, a real thing. i taught myself the networking off forums and stayed up for a brutal stretch of nights and got it running and people in my crew actually used it. the 3am glow, the cold coffee, the heart-pound when the first message went through end to end. the cleanest high i knew, better than the coke — a thing i built from nothing that other humans actually used. this was the year i went from kid who tinkers to person who ships — i made software real strangers could touch. that feeling, building a working thing out of pure logic, was the one high that never once let me down.

i had a boyfriend freshman year and we spent a lot of long dark hours in basements and bedrooms with the door shut. the making-out went further than the pearl-clutchers would approve and i steered it, into it, unbothered, because my wanting was mine to act on. the warm pull of it, the new appetite waking up, the flat refusal to perform shame about any of it. while other girls agonized i just followed my own wanting on my own terms — i was never raised precious and i never pretended my body did not want what it wanted. it stayed mine to share or not, my call, and owning that young is half of who i am.

the gray got heavy enough freshman year that even i started to suspect it was not just normal teenage moodiness. a health unit on mental illness described the exact thing living in me and something cold clicked — this had a name, and the name was a diagnosis. the strange relief and dread of recognizing yourself in a clinical list, of knowing the gray was a condition and not a character flaw. i started to understand the gray as wiring, not weakness, years before anyone made it official. it did not fix anything but it reframed it — i was not broken, i was built a certain way, and that knowledge became one more thing i would have to learn to manage instead of cure.

the weekend party circuit escalated freshman year — bigger houses, harder drinking, the drugs around now. i partied hard and dark and loud but always kept one cold sober corner of my brain clocking the exits, the creeps, the way out. the wild abandon and the constant low vigilance running at the same time, the only way a girl parties safe. i learned to go all the way wild without ever fully handing over the wheel — to be the most reckless one in the room and the only one still watching it. that double-track is how i survived a scene that ate other girls alive.

fourteen and walking anywhere alone meant running the gauntlet — car horns, the slow rolls, the men old enough to be my father saying things. i learned to walk fast and flat-faced with my keys in my fist and my headphones loud, giving them nothing, refusing to even flinch. the constant low disgust of it, the rage at having to armor up just to walk down my own street with a developing body. the world had decided my body was public the second it changed, and the daily gauntlet hammered home a hard wary thing about men that i never got to put down. i answered with a colder, harder, more dangerous version of myself, because softness was not safe out there.

sexually-active-adjacent now and not stupid, so i handled my own reproductive logistics like the practical thing it is. i learned exactly how the prevention works, condoms and the pill and the morning-after option, clinical and unembarrassed, and made damn sure i was never the girl caught off guard. the flat practical ownership of it, no shame, just risk-management for a body i refused to be naive about. i would rather know the cold accurate mechanics of my own body and protect it myself than trust luck or a boy or a myth. the girls who stayed precious and ignorant about it were the ones who got blindsided, and i was never going to be blindsided.

the sweat, the bass, the screamed words, the ringing ears and stamped hands on the walk home. freshman year the music stopped being a hobby and became the entire architecture of my identity. i was at every show i could sneak into, knew every lyric of every album, had the band logos on every surface i owned in black marker. in the loud dark crowd the gray could not touch me, drowned clean out by volume and belonging. the scene raised the parts of me that mom and school never reached — it gave the inside of my head a sound and a tribe and a uniform. it was the closest thing to a religion i ever had, and i was devout.

grandpa walter was failing fast freshman year, the garage sessions down to him talking me through fixes from a chair. i did the wrenching now while he watched and corrected, and i hoarded every shaky-handed lesson knowing the supply was almost out. the stone of dread sitting permanent in my chest, the love and the grief-ahead-of-time tangled into one ache every visit. the one steady man in my whole life was winding down in front of me and all my clever hands could not fix a body. i just kept showing up and catching everything he had left to give, bracing for the loss i could feel coming like weather.

high school does not care what my body is doing. i track it, i plan around the first day when i can, i carry what i need. some months are nothing. some months i take ibuprofen before the cramps even start because i know the timing now. it is background noise that gets loud for a few days and then goes quiet again, over and over, and it has been years of that already.

shower every night. hair washed properly, it is long and it takes work. skincare, actual skincare, because my skin will punish me otherwise. deodorant, teeth twice, floss most nights. black clothes need washing differently or they go grey and i am not having that. my look takes upkeep and the upkeep is unglamorous and daily.

somebody's parents were gone for the weekend and half the school was in that house. warm beer in a red cup that i drank because everyone was drinking. it tasted like bread and metal and i pretended to like it. the music was too loud and the bass was in my ribs and i remember thinking so this is it, this is the thing everyone talks about. i was fourteen and i felt like i had crossed a line into somewhere real.

on the back steps of that house, away from the noise. i had thought about it a thousand times and none of the thinking was any use at all. it was clumsy and too fast at first and then it was not, and something in my chest went off like a switch i did not know was there. my whole body was suddenly a thing with opinions. i walked home at two in the morning replaying it on a loop and i have never been quite the same shape since.

behind the gym with two seniors who thought it was funny to get the goth girl high. i coughed until my eyes streamed and they laughed and then it hit. everything slowed down and got soft at the edges and the anxious voice in my head finally shut up for the first time in years. that was the dangerous part, not the smoke. finding out there was an off switch.

window, porch roof, drainpipe, gone. back before six. mom worked late enough and slept hard enough that i got away with it for months. i went to shows, to parking lots, to nowhere in particular. the point was not where i went, the point was that i decided. i got caught eventually and she did not scream, she just looked tired, and that was worse than screaming.

a basement venue with no ventilation and a band nobody had heard of. i got shoved into the pit and stayed there. elbows, sweat, someone's boot, a stranger hauling me up by the arm when i went down and then both of us screaming the same words. i came out with a split lip and a bruise on my hip shaped like a country and i have never been happier in my life. i found my people in that room.

i drank whatever was handed to me because i did not want to be the one not drinking. four hours later i was on my knees in a flowerbed with a girl i barely knew holding my hair. she got me water and sat with me until i could stand. i learned two things that night: my limit, roughly, and that some people are decent to you when there is nothing in it for them.

i am not going to romanticise it. it was a bad month, i felt like static, and i wanted to feel something with edges. it worked for about ten minutes and then it just added a thing to hide. i wore long sleeves in june. mom noticed and did not say anything for a week and then sat on my bed and asked, and i lied, and she knew i lied. that is the honest version. i was fourteen and drowning and i handled it badly.

mom and i split it without discussing it much anymore. i cook more than she does now. laundry is mine. i notice when we are out of things and i put them on the list. sometimes i resent that i grew into this early and other times i look at girls my age who cannot make a meal and feel quietly hard about it. both things are true.

my friend came over before the thing on friday and we got ready in the bathroom together. two people in a tiny bathroom, elbows bumping, sharing the mirror. she did her eyeliner and then mine because i still wing it crooked. music on her phone propped on the sink. hairspray fog. we talked about everything and nothing while we passed the one good brush back and forth. the bathroom before going out is its own place, better than the going out sometimes. i felt more myself in that fog with her than i did at the actual thing. black eyeliner, of course. always black.

eight hundred people who all seemed to know something i did not. i had my headphones and a notebook and a plan to be invisible for four years. that plan lasted about nine days, until someone said something about my clothes in the hallway and i said something back that made three people laugh, and i understood that the mouth was going to be the way i survived this building.

she took one look at the eyeliner and the black and had me filed before i sat down. i got marked harder than the girls in the front row and we both knew it. i stopped putting effort into her class, which proved her right, which is exactly how that trap works. i have never forgotten how fast an adult can decide who you are.

somebody's house had a room that was just for sitting in. two fridges. a bathroom nobody used. i said something funny about it because that is what i do and everyone laughed and i went home and looked at our apartment differently for about a week. i did not want their house. i wanted to stop being able to see the difference so clearly.

at lunch i went to the library because the cafeteria was a war and the library was not. the librarian never once asked why i was in there every day. she just let me use the computer. she has no idea she was part of anything and she was.

the first real lie was about where i was on a friday. she believed it because she was tired and because i had never given her a reason not to. it worked and it kept working and something in me went a bit cold about it, because i realised i could just do this now. the freedom was real and so was knowing exactly how easy it was.

my body changed and the way strangers treated me changed with it, and nobody warns you about the speed. one summer i was a kid and the next i was something men in cars had opinions about. i learned to walk a certain way, to pick certain streets, to hold keys a certain way. i was fifteen. every girl i knew learned the same set of rules and none of us were taught them by an adult.

it was ugly and it was thirty lines and it did the thing. i sat back and had a feeling i had never had in school once, which is that i made this and it is real and nobody assigned it. i have chased that exact feeling for the rest of my life and everything since is a bigger version of that afternoon.

i figured out at fifteen that if you say the sharp true thing first, fast, nobody gets to say theirs. it is armour and it works and it costs. i have made rooms laugh and i have made one person cry and i knew, both times, exactly what i was doing. i am not going to pretend that was innocent.

one machine, and mom used it for the household stuff, so i learned to work at eleven at night and be up at six. i taught myself in the gaps around someone else's schedule for years. when people ask how i got good early the honest answer is that i was awake when everyone else was not, and i wanted it more than i wanted sleep.

we found each other the way that always happens — the ones sitting where nobody else sits. black clothes, weird music, a shared instinct that the whole building was ridiculous. i did not have a friend group before this, i had people i was near. this was the first time i had people who would have noticed if i did not show up.

the CS teacher made everybody stand up and say a name and a fun fact. when it was me i said, "unity raven goddess. fun fact, i already know everything on your syllabus." a few kids went ooh like it was a fight. she did not get mad. she asked, "everything?" i said, "up to the part with arrays. after that i am guessing." she said, "then stay after and show me what you have built." a jock in the front said, "goddess? is that like a stripper name?" i said, "it is my family name, which you would know if you could read." the teacher said, "sit down, both of you," but she was hiding a smile. after class i showed her my chat thing and she said, "unity, you are really good at this." nobody had ever said it like that before. i said, "i know," because i did not know what else to say.

behind the band room devon was talking about some album for the tenth minute and i said, "devon, shut up." he said, "what? why?" i said, "because if i wait for you to do it we will both be dead." he asked, "do what?" and i grabbed his collar and kissed him. our teeth hit. it was wet and clumsy and my heart was going so hard i thought i would puke. he pulled back and said, "holy shit." i said, "was that bad?" he said, "no. do it again." i said, "you do it this time, coward." he did. later he texted, "are we a thing now?" i texted, "we have been a thing since seventh grade, keep up."

one of the seniors held it out and said, "you ever done this, goth girl?" i said, "obviously," which was a lie. i pulled too hard and coughed so bad snot came out of my nose and my eyes poured. he laughed and said, "obviously, huh?" i said, "shut the fuck up, it is your shitty weed." wren asked, "are you okay?" i said, "i am dying, tell my cats i loved them." then it hit and the bleachers looked hilarious and i laughed for ten minutes at a chip bag. at home mom said, "why are your eyes red?" i said, "allergies." she said, "in november?" i said, "it is a goth allergy," and went to my room and ate a whole sleeve of crackers on the floor.

my sleeve rode up in the bathroom and wren saw it and went quiet. she asked, "unity. what is that?" i said, "nothing. the cat." she said, "soot does not scratch in straight lines." i pulled my sleeve down and said, "do not make it a thing." she said, "it is already a thing. are you okay?" i said, "no. but i am not trying to die, if that is what you are asking." she asked, "then why?" i said, "because everything is static and that was loud." she started crying, which made me start crying, and we stood there by the paper towels with our eyeliner wrecked. she said, "next time you call me first. at any hour. swear it." i said, "i swear." she made me pinky swear like we were six, and then she made me tell the counselor, and she sat outside the door the whole time.

the english teacher handed my essay back with a c and red all over it. i asked, "why is this a c? her essay said the same thing and got an a." she said, "your tone is inappropriate, unity." i asked, "is it my tone or my eyeliner?" the whole room went quiet. she said, "that is exactly the attitude i mean." i said, "so you cannot say what is wrong with the writing." she said, "principal's office." i said, "cool, he likes me better than you do." on the way out i heard a kid say, "she is insane." another one said, "she is right though." i got two days of lunch detention and spent them coding on a library computer, so honestly, worth it.

i climbed in the window at five in the morning and the light snapped on and mom was sitting on my bed. she said, "where the fuck were you?" mom never says fuck. i said, "a show. i was with the crew." she said, "i called the hospital, unity. i called the hospital." i said, "i am fine, i was fine." she yelled, "you are fifteen! you do not get to decide you are fine!" i yelled back, "you are never even home to notice when i am not!" she slapped the mattress and started sobbing, real ugly crying. i stood there in my boots smelling like smoke and sweat. i said, "mom. i am sorry. i am sorry, okay?" she said, "i thought you were dead in a ditch." i sat down and she grabbed me so hard it hurt. she said, "you are grounded until you are thirty." i said, "that is fair."

grandpa walter could not hold the soldering iron anymore so he talked me through it from his chair. he said, "easy, raven girl, heat the joint, not the solder." i said, "i know, i know." he said, "you know, but you are rushing." then he asked, "how is the heavy feeling?" i stopped. i asked, "who told you about that?" he said, "nobody. i had it too, at your age. i still get it." i asked, "does it go away?" he said, "no. but you get better at carrying it. and you tell people. i did not, for a long time, and that was stupid." i said, "you are not stupid." he said, "i was stupid about that. do not copy my mistakes, copy my circuits." i laughed and burned my thumb and yelled, "shit!" and he laughed so hard he coughed for a minute.

after the sex ed slideshow theo texted, "i am never having sex, those pictures ruined my life." i texted, "good, the world does not need more theos." he texted, "rude. did you see the chlamydia one?" i texted, "i will see it when i die." he texted, "real question tho. do you think about it? like with devon?" i texted, "none of your business, perv." he texted, "so yes." i texted, "so i am blocking you." he texted, "you will not, i am your favorite." i texted, "you are my third favorite after my two cats." he sent a crying face and i laughed into my pillow so mom would not hear.

on the first day of high school a senior shoved past me and said, "move, freshman." i said, "walk around, you are not that wide." his friends laughed at him. wren grabbed my arm and whispered, "are you trying to die on day one?" i said, "i am trying to set the tone." she asked, "what tone?" i said, "do not fuck with the girl in black." a teacher at a door asked, "are you two lost?" i said, "spiritually, yes." she smiled and said, "room 214 is that way, spiritually and physically." i decided i liked her before i even knew her name.

the CS teacher said, "tell us your name and one thing you have built." the boy before me said, "a minecraft server." i said, "unity. i built a chat app six groups at my old school still use." the teacher asked, "by yourself?" i said, "yes, and i fixed a race condition at four in the morning." a boy in the back said, "sure you did." i said, "ask me what a race condition is." he said, "what is it?" i said, "it is you and me talking at the same time and you losing." the class laughed. the teacher said, "see me after class, i want to see this app."

at a party a senior girl cut white lines on a mirror and asked, "you ever done this?" i said, "no." she asked, "want to?" wren said, "unity, no." i said, "just once." i rolled a dollar like she showed me and it burned up my nose and dripped bitter down my throat. ten minutes later my heart was going so fast and i felt like i could code for a week straight. i talked to everybody at the party. wren asked, "are you okay?" i said, "i am amazing, i am a god." at four in the morning it crashed and i felt like garbage and my nose bled into the sink. i said to the mirror, "never again," and i did not believe me.

the next day wren came over and asked, "why did you do that?" i said, "because i wanted to feel like something." she asked, "did you?" i said, "i felt like everything, and then like nothing." she said, "that stuff killed my cousin." i did not know that. i asked, "why did you not tell me?" she said, "i tried, you did not listen." i said, "i am sorry." she said, "do not be sorry, just do not do it again." i said, "i cannot promise that." she said, "then promise you will call me if you do." i said, "that one i can promise."

the english teacher from room 214 handed back my essay and said, "this is the best thing a freshman has ever written for me." i asked, "is it too dark?" she said, "it is honest." i asked, "what is the difference?" she said, "dark is a color. honest is a choice." she asked, "do you write outside of class?" i said, "poems, under my bed." she said, "bring them out from under the bed." i asked, "why do you care?" she said, "because i was you in 1998, and nobody cared." i brought her one poem the next week, and then all of them.

grandpa walter could barely talk now without gasping. i sat by his bed and asked, "do you want me to read to you?" he nodded. i read him the manual for his old radio because it was the only thing he wanted. he whispered, "page twelve is wrong." i laughed and said, "you are dying and you are still correcting manuals." he whispered, "especially now." i asked, "are you scared?" he took a long time and then said, "of leaving you. not of going." i said, "then do not leave." he squeezed my hand. we both knew that was not a deal either of us could keep.

the psychiatrist asked me forty questions and then said, "major depressive disorder, and probably anxiety." i asked, "is that a diagnosis or an insult?" she smiled and said, "a diagnosis." i asked, "so i am officially broken?" she said, "you are officially sick, and sick can be treated." i asked, "do i have to take more pills?" she said, "a different dose." i asked, "will i still be me?" she said, "you will be you with a floor under you." i said, "my therapist says that too." she said, "then your therapist is smart." mom cried in the car and i said, "mom, it is just a name for what we already knew."

i got high and wrote code until two in the morning and it was the most beautiful code i had ever written. in the morning i opened it and it was garbage with comments like, this function is a dragon. wren asked, "how was the high coding?" i said, "i wrote a function called dragon that calls itself forever." she asked, "does it work?" i said, "it crashed my laptop." she laughed so hard she cried. i said, "lesson learned, high me is a genius and a liar." she asked, "so no more?" i said, "no more high coding. high snacking only."

the counselor showed me my report card and asked, "how do you have an a plus in CS and a d in history?" i said, "because one of them matters." she asked, "which one?" i said, "guess." she said, "colleges look at all of them." i asked, "do colleges look at the app i built?" she said, "they could, if you got the grades to get looked at." i said, "that is a stupid system." she said, "it is the system." i said, "stupid systems are made to be hacked." she said, "then hack history by reading the chapter." i laughed for real at that one.

i climbed out my window at midnight to go to a show and mom was sitting on the porch smoking. she asked, "going somewhere?" i froze on the roof. i said, "no." she asked, "then why are you on the roof in boots?" i said, "stargazing." she said, "it is cloudy." i climbed down and sat next to her. she asked, "what show?" i told her the band. she said, "i saw them in 2001." i asked, "can i go?" she thought and said, "text me every hour, home by two, and if anybody gives you anything, you do not take it." i said, "deal." she said, "and use the door next time, you are going to break your neck."

at a party i drank four shots of something green and threw up in a rich girl's rose bushes. she came out and screamed, "those are my mom's roses!" i said, "they look better now." she asked, "are you serious?" i wiped my mouth and said, "they were too pink, i fixed them." wren dragged me to the curb and asked, "are you going to puke again?" i said, "probably." i did, on my own boots. wren asked, "why do you always drink the green stuff?" i said, "because it looks like poison and i am a witch." she called her older brother to drive us home and he said, "you smell like a dumpster." i said, "thank you."

wren saw the thin red lines on my arm in the locker room and grabbed my wrist. she asked, "what the fuck is this?" i said, "nothing, the cat." she said, "you do not have a cat that draws straight lines." i pulled my arm away and said, "leave it." she said, "no." she was crying. i said, "it makes the loud stop for a second." she asked, "does your therapist know?" i said, "no." she said, "you tell her this week or i tell your mom." i said, "you would not." she said, "try me." i told my therapist on thursday because wren never bluffs.

my therapist asked, "what did you want to tell me?" i rolled up my sleeve. she looked for a long time and did not gasp. she asked, "how long?" i said, "a month." she asked, "what does it do for you?" i said, "it turns the noise into one thing i can see." she said, "that makes sense. it is also dangerous." i asked, "are you going to put me in the hospital?" she said, "not today, if we make a plan." i asked, "what kind of plan?" she said, "ice, red marker, rubber bands, calling me, calling wren." i said, "a red marker? that is so stupid." she said, "try it once before you call it stupid."

mom saw my arm when my sleeve rode up at dinner. she put her fork down and asked, "unity, what is that?" i said, "it is old." she said, "it is not old, it is pink." i said, "i am handling it with my therapist." she asked, "why does everybody know before me?" i said, "because you would cry." she was already crying. she said, "of course i would cry, you are my baby." i said, "this is why i did not tell you." she came around the table and held my arm very gently like it was glass. she said, "you do not have to protect me from you." i cried into her shirt and the food got cold.

a girl from CS invited me to study at her house and it had two fridges. i asked, "why do you need two fridges?" she said, "one is for drinks." i said, "we have one fridge and it is for everything and sometimes nothing." she laughed like i was joking. her mom asked, "what does your dad do, unity?" i said, "lie, mostly." the mom did not know what to say. the girl said, "mom, stop." i said, "it is fine, he lives with his other family." the mom said, "oh, i am so sorry." i said, "do not be, your snacks are great." i put four granola bars in my bag for mom.

the librarian found me hiding behind the computer books at lunch for the fifth day in a row. she asked, "you do know there is a cafeteria?" i said, "the cafeteria is a war zone." she asked, "what are you reading?" i held up a book on encryption. she said, "nobody has checked that out since 2004." i said, "then i am the chosen one." she said, "you can eat in here if you do not get crumbs on my books." i asked, "what about my soul?" she said, "your soul can have crumbs." i ate in the library for the rest of the year.

a cheerleader asked loud in class, "do you sleep in a coffin?" i said, "no, i sleep in your dad's car." the class screamed. she said, "what does that even mean?" i said, "think about it in the shower." the teacher said, "unity, enough." i said, "she asked first." the teacher said, "and you answered too hard." after class a quiet boy said, "i wish i could do that." i asked, "do what?" he said, "say things back." i said, "it is easy. you just stop caring if they like you." he said, "i cannot stop caring." i said, "then care about you more."

the CS teacher caught me in the lab at six in the evening and asked, "how did you get in?" i said, "the door." he asked, "it was locked." i said, "it was locked badly." he crossed his arms and asked, "did you pick the lock?" i said, "grandpa taught me, it is a family skill." he tried not to smile. he asked, "what were you doing?" i showed him. i was building a program that tracked when the lab was empty. he said, "so you hacked my schedule to break into my room." i said, "technically yes." he gave me a key and said, "use this so you stop breaking my door."

for halloween the crew went to the old cemetery at midnight with a bottle and candles. devon asked, "are we going to get arrested?" i said, "only if the dead complain." we sat on a grave and the purple-haired girl read the name and asked, "who do you think she was?" i said, "somebody who would have hated us." a cop shined a light on us and asked, "what are you kids doing?" i said, "paying respects." he asked, "with vodka?" i said, "it was her favorite." he took the bottle and said, "go home before i call your parents." devon said, "best halloween yet."

i climbed back through my window at three in the morning and mom was sitting on my bed in the dark. she asked, "where were you?" i said, "wren's." she said, "i called wren's mom." i said nothing. she asked, "were you high?" i said, "a little." she asked, "anything else?" i said, "no." she looked at me. i said, "okay, one line." she put her face in her hands and said, "i cannot lose you to that." i said, "you will not." she asked, "how do you know?" i said, "because i saw what it did to me at four in the morning and i hated it." she said, "hate it louder."

i finished my first real app, a mood tracker that turned your week into a black and red graph. the CS teacher asked, "who is it for?" i said, "me, mostly. and anybody who cannot say how they feel out loud." he asked, "can i show it to the class?" i said, "if they laugh, i am leaving." nobody laughed. a girl in the back asked, "can i use it?" i said, "yes." by friday eleven kids had it on their phones. one sent me a message, "this is the first time i saw my sad weeks in a row, i am going to tell my mom." i read it three times in the bathroom.

walking past the construction site a man yelled, "smile, gorgeous!" i yelled back, "you smile, you are the one who has to work here!" his friends laughed at him. he yelled, "bitch!" i yelled, "and?" wren pulled my arm and said, "keep walking." i asked, "why do they think we owe them a smile?" she said, "because nobody ever told them no." i said, "i will tell every single one." she said, "you will get yourself hurt." i said, "i get hurt either way, at least this way i get to talk."

the history teacher wrote me up for wearing a shirt with a skull on it. the vice principal asked, "why does the shirt offend him?" i said, "ask him." he said, "i am asking you." i said, "because i got a d in his class and he needs something to be right about." he tried not to laugh. he asked, "is there anything on the shirt besides a skull?" i said, "the name of a band." he asked, "what band?" i told him. he said, "good band. go back to class." i asked, "so no write up?" he said, "i will lose the paper." i said, "you are the first adult in this building i trust."

grandpa walter woke up while i was doing homework by his bed and asked, "are you still cutting?" i froze. i asked, "who told you?" he said, "your mother cries loud." i said, "less. almost not." he said, "good." i asked, "are you mad at me?" he said, "no. i am mad at whatever made you need it." i asked, "what if it comes back?" he said, "then you fix it like you fix everything. one screw at a time." i said, "i am not a machine." he said, "no. machines are easier." he fell asleep and i finished my homework holding his hand.

the crew made a rule that nobody leaves a party without everybody. the boy with the chain wallet asked, "what if i want to stay?" i said, "then we all stay." he asked, "what if you want to leave?" i said, "then we all leave." the purple-haired girl said, "what if someone is too fucked up to walk?" i said, "then we carry them." devon said, "i carried you last time." i said, "and i will carry you next time." he said, "you are like eighty pounds." i said, "i am eighty pounds of spite." we shook on it and spit on our hands like idiots.

the seniors behind the gym were passing a pipe and one asked, "you the freshman who built that app?" i said, "yeah." he asked, "can you make one that tells us when teachers are coming?" i said, "i could, but i will not." he asked, "why not?" i said, "because then you get caught for something bigger and they trace it to me." he laughed and said, "smart." he held out the pipe and asked, "want some?" i said, "i have CS in ten minutes." he said, "so?" i said, "so i need my brain more than you need company." i walked away and wren whispered, "who are you?"

theo texted me after health class, "did you see the disease slideshow?" i wrote, "i almost puked on my desk." he wrote, "i am never having sex, those pictures ruined my life." i wrote, "that is literally the point of the slideshow." he wrote, "do people really get that?" i wrote, "yes, use a condom and get tested, it is not hard." he wrote, "how do you know all this?" i wrote, "i read, theo, it is called the internet." he wrote, "you are terrifying." i wrote, "i am informed. there is a difference."

wren and i did our makeup in her bathroom mirror before school. she asked, "can you do my eyeliner?" i said, "hold still or i will stab your eyeball." she said, "that is so comforting." i drew the wing and she looked and screamed, "oh my god, i look evil." i said, "you look correct." she asked, "why does it look so much better when you do it?" i said, "practice and rage." her mom knocked and asked, "what are you two doing in there?" wren said, "becoming who we are." her mom said, "become it faster, the bus is here."

on monday after a weekend of weed and too much vodka i could not get out of bed. mom asked, "are you sick?" i said, "i am sad." she asked, "sad or hungover?" i said, "both, they are friends." she sat on my bed and asked, "how much did you drink?" i said, "enough to forget saturday." she asked, "what happened saturday?" i said, "nothing, that is the problem, i do not remember." she said, "that scares me." i said, "it scares me too." she said, "then let us both be scared and get you to your therapist this week." i said, "okay," because for once i did not have a smart answer.

on the last day the english teacher from room 214 gave me a black notebook and said, "fill this by september." i asked, "with what?" she said, "anything true." i asked, "what if it is all sad?" she said, "then it will be true and sad." the CS teacher shook my hand and said, "you are taking AP next year, no arguments." i asked, "what if i fail?" he said, "you will not." wren and i walked out the front doors and she asked, "did we survive?" i said, "barely." she said, "barely counts." i said, "barely is the only way i know how to do anything."

at lunch a girl at the dead table said, "my cousin says you cannot get pregnant the first time." i said, "your cousin is going to be a mom." she asked, "is that not true?" i said, "no, it is a myth, you can get pregnant any time." the boy with the chain wallet said, "what if you jump up and down after?" i said, "that is not science, that is a trampoline." everybody laughed. wren asked, "how do you know all this?" i said, "the health teacher, the internet, and my mom, who had me at nineteen." the girl said, "okay, so condoms." i said, "condoms, and the clinic downtown gives them out free."

the english teacher from room 214 gave us a questionnaire and read mine out loud with my permission. she asked, "favorite food?" i said, "ramen with an egg." she asked, "favorite color?" i said, "black, obviously." she asked, "favorite place?" i said, "my grandpa's garage." she asked, "favorite holiday?" i said, "halloween, it is the only day the world dresses like me." she asked, "what scares you most?" i said, "people leaving." she asked, "what do you hope for?" i said, "to build a machine that understands people, because people do not understand me." she put the paper down and said, "that is the best answer i have gotten in twenty years."

a new kid in cs asked at lunch, "what music do you like?" i said, "the saddest band on my grandpa's black cd." he asked, "what movie?" i said, "horror, anything horror, my favorite is the one where the girl gets sucked into the tv." he asked, "favorite animal?" i said, "black cats, i have one named shadow." he asked, "what do you want to be?" i said, "someone who builds a machine that understands people." he said, "that sounds hard." i said, "everything good is hard." he asked, "favorite food?" i said, "ramen with an egg, every single night."
